query.title: The typeof operator
query.explanation: `typeof null` returns the string "object". This is a long-standing bug in the original `typeof` table, not evidence that `null` is an object you can read properties from. `null === null` is the test that actually recognizes null, and reading a property off null throws.

query.title: The typeof operator and its result strings
query.explanation: `typeof` returns a string naming the operand's type, and the undefined value is reported as the string "undefined". It does not return the undefined value itself, and it does not throw. `null` is the nearby value that does not get its own typeof tag.

questions.prompt: What does `typeof` report for a function?

query.title: The typeof operator and its result strings
query.explanation: Functions are objects, but `typeof` has a dedicated result, the string "function", for any callable. "object" is what `typeof` says for ordinary objects and arrays, so it is the wrong tag here. There is no "callable" result.

query.title: The typeof operator
query.explanation: Arrays are objects, and `typeof` has no separate "array" result, so `typeof []` is "object". `Array.isArray` is the check that distinguishes an array from a plain object. "list" is not a JavaScript typeof tag.

query.title: The typeof operator and JavaScript types
query.explanation: `NaN` is a numeric value, the IEEE-754 not-a-number bit pattern, so `typeof NaN` is "number". It is not its own type and it is not undefined. `Number.isNaN` is how you test for it, because a typeof check cannot.

questions.prompt: What does `typeof` do with an identifier that was never declared?

query.title: The typeof operator and unresolvable names
query.explanation: `typeof` has a special case for an unresolvable reference: it returns the string "undefined" and does not throw. Reading that same identifier without `typeof` throws a ReferenceError. A `let` or `const` that exists but is still in the temporal dead zone is different: `typeof` on that binding still throws.

query.title: Loose equality and type coercion
query.explanation: The `==` operator converts operands of different types before comparing. A numeric comparison converts the string "1" with `ToNumber`, and `1 == 1` is true. This is not a type match: `===` on the same operands is false.

query.title: Equality operators: strict vs loose comparison
query.explanation: `===` returns false when the types differ, and it does not convert the string to a number first. A number and a string are different types even when they look like the same digit. `==` is the operator that would coerce and return true here.

query.title: Loose equality (==) and type coercion rules
query.explanation: Abstract equality defines `null == undefined` as true, and it does not convert either value to 0 or to a string first. No other value loosely equals null: `null == 0` and `null == false` are both false. `===` still treats null and undefined as different.

query.title: Strict vs loose equality across types
query.explanation: `===` requires the same type and the same value. `null` and `undefined` are different types, so the comparison is false and nothing is thrown. The loose operator `==` is the one that treats this pair as equal.

query.title: Loose equality (==) and type coercion
query.explanation: When `==` compares a boolean to a number, it converts the boolean with `ToNumber`. `ToNumber(true)` is 1, so the comparison becomes `1 == 1`. `true === 1` stays false because the types still differ.

query.title: Loose equality (==) and type coercion
query.explanation: `==` converts the boolean before comparing it with a number. `ToNumber(false)` is 0, so `false == 0` is true. Strict equality does not do that conversion: `false === 0` is false.

query.title: Loose equality (==) and type coercion
query.explanation: Both sides of `==` are converted to numbers when a boolean meets a string. `ToNumber("")` is 0 and `ToNumber(false)` is 0, so the comparison is true. `false === ""` is false, and `Boolean("")` being false is a different rule from this equality.

query.title: Loose equality (==) type coercion
query.explanation: Abstract equality converts `[]` with `ToPrimitive` to the empty string, then to the number 0, and it converts `false` to 0 as well. The comparison is therefore true. The array is still truthy in a boolean context: `Boolean([])` is true, and `[] === false` is false.

query.title: Strict equality and special numeric values
query.explanation: IEEE-754 says NaN compares unequal to every value, including itself, and both `===` and `==` follow that rule. A self-check with `===` can never detect NaN. `Object.is(NaN, NaN)` and `Number.isNaN` are the tests that return true.

choices.text: Number.isNaN returns true and isNaN returns false
Number.isNaN returns false and isNaN returns true

query.title: Global isNaN vs Number.isNaN: coercion differences
query.explanation: `Number.isNaN` returns true only when the argument is already the number NaN, so the string "foo" is false. The global `isNaN` converts its argument with `ToNumber` first, `ToNumber("foo")` is NaN, and that coerced result makes `isNaN("foo")` true. They are not aliases.

query.title: Object.is and SameValue equality
query.explanation: `Object.is` uses the SameValue comparison, which treats NaN as the same value as NaN. That is the deliberate difference from `===`, which is false for this pair. `Object.is` is not a general deep-equal for objects.

choices.text: Object.is is false and === is true
Object.is is true and === is false

query.title: Equality comparison: Object.is vs strict equality
query.explanation: `===` follows ordinary equality, which treats positive zero and negative zero as the same number, so `+0 === -0` is true. `Object.is` uses SameValue and keeps the sign, so `Object.is(+0, -0)` is false. Signed zero still behaves like zero in arithmetic such as `1 / -0`, which is `-Infinity`.

query.title: Floating-point number precision and equality
query.explanation: JavaScript numbers are IEEE-754 binary floats, and 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation. Their sum is a value slightly larger than 0.3, so `===` against the literal 0.3 is false. The addition does not throw, and `===` is not broken for integers.

query.title: Number() conversion of strings
query.explanation: `Number` converts its argument with `ToNumber`. An empty string, and a string of only whitespace, converts to 0 rather than to NaN. A non-numeric string such as "10px" is the case that becomes NaN.

query.title: Converting strings to numbers with Number()
query.explanation: `Number` requires the whole string, after trimming whitespace, to be a numeric literal. The trailing "px" makes "10px" invalid, so the result is NaN, not the leading 10. `parseInt("10px", 10)` is the call that stops at the first bad character and returns 10.

query.title: String-to-integer parsing with parseInt
query.explanation: `parseInt` reads a numeric prefix and stops at the first character that is not valid in the given radix. With radix 10, "10px" yields 10 and the "px" is ignored. `Number("10px")` does not ignore that suffix: it returns NaN. Nothing here throws.

query.title: parseInt string-to-integer parsing and radix
query.explanation: The radix argument 10 forces a decimal parse, so the leading 0 is just a digit and the value is 8. Older engines sometimes treated a leading zero as octal when the radix was omitted, which made "08" look invalid. With an explicit 10, that octal reading does not apply, and the result is not 0 or NaN.

query.title: Parsing numbers from strings with parseFloat
query.explanation: `parseFloat` parses a decimal prefix and stops at the first character that cannot continue the number. "3.14abc" therefore becomes 3.14, not NaN and not the original string. `Number("3.14abc")` is NaN, because `Number` refuses a trailing suffix.

query.title: Unary plus and type coercion to number
query.explanation: Unary `+` converts with `ToNumber`. An array's primitive form is its `toString` join, an empty array joins to "", and `ToNumber("")` is 0. The expression does not stay an array, and it is not NaN. A plain object is the value that becomes NaN under the same operator.

query.title: Unary plus and ToNumber conversion of objects
query.explanation: Unary `+` asks the object for a primitive. A plain object's `toString` is "[object Object]", and that string is not numeric, so the result is NaN. It does not become 0 the way `+[]` does, and the result is not the string "[object Object]" itself.

query.title: The String() conversion function
query.explanation: `String` has an explicit case for null: it returns the four-character string "null". It does not return an empty string, and it does not throw the way `` `${null.missing}` `` would. `String(undefined)` is the separate string "undefined".

query.title: String() conversion function
query.explanation: `String` converts undefined to the string "undefined", not to an empty string and not to "null". The conversion does not throw. Concatenation does the same conversion: `"" + undefined` is also "undefined".

query.title: Boolean() conversion and truthiness
query.explanation: `Boolean` uses the falsy list, and the empty string is on it, so `Boolean("")` is false. The result is an actual boolean, not the empty string echoed back. A string of the word "false", or a string of spaces, is non-empty and therefore true.

query.title: Boolean() conversion and truthiness
query.explanation: Any non-empty string is truthy, including the characters f-a-l-s-e. `Boolean` does not parse the string the way `JSON.parse` would, so it does not produce false. Only the empty string is a falsy string.

query.title: Truthy and falsy values with Boolean()
query.explanation: Objects, arrays included, are truthy. `Boolean` does not convert the array to a string or a number first, so the empty array is true even though `[] == false` is also true. Emptiness is not the same rule as falsiness.

query.title: Boolean() conversion and truthy/falsy values
query.explanation: 0 is on the falsy list, along with -0, NaN, "", null, undefined, and false. `Boolean(0)` is therefore the boolean false, not the number 0 left in place. A non-zero number, including a negative one, is truthy.

query.title: Truthy and falsy conversion with Boolean()
query.explanation: Every object is truthy, including an object with no own properties. `Boolean` does not look inside the object and does not use the `ToNumber` path that makes `+{}` NaN. `null` is the empty-looking value that is falsy, and null is not an object you can use this way.

query.title: Nullish coalescing operator (??)
query.explanation: The `??` operator returns the right operand only when the left operand is null or undefined. `null` is nullish, so the result is "x". It does not throw, and it does not return null once a right-hand fallback is present.

query.title: Nullish coalescing operator
query.explanation: `??` replaces only null and undefined. 0 is a real value, so the expression keeps 0 and does not evaluate the fallback. `||` is the operator that would treat 0 as missing and return "x".

query.title: Nullish coalescing operator
query.explanation: The empty string is falsy but not nullish, so `??` keeps it. The right-hand "x" is not used. `"" || "x"` returns "x" because `||` treats every falsy value as a reason to take the fallback.

query.title: Nullish coalescing operator
query.explanation: `undefined` is nullish, so `??` returns the right operand, "x". The result is not left as undefined, and the expression does not throw. 0 and "" would have been kept, because only null and undefined trigger the fallback.

query.title: Optional chaining operator (?.)
query.explanation: Optional chaining stops when the base is null or undefined and yields undefined instead of reading the property. `null.prop` without the question mark throws a TypeError. The result is the undefined value, not the string "undefined", and not null.

questions.prompt: What does an optional call on `null` do?

choices.text: Throws a TypeError: fn is not a function
Returns null, the value of fn
Returns false, since fn is falsy

query.title: Optional chaining call syntax (?.())
query.explanation: When the callee is null or undefined, `fn?.()` does not perform the call and the expression evaluates to undefined. A bare `fn()` would throw a TypeError because null is not callable. The short-circuit applies only to null and undefined: a non-nullish value that is not a function still throws when the call proceeds.

query.title: Logical OR operator and truthiness
query.explanation: `||` returns the first operand if it is truthy, otherwise the second. 0 is falsy, so the result is "fallback", and the result is that string rather than the boolean false. `??` would have kept the 0, because 0 is not nullish.

query.title: Logical AND operator and short-circuit evaluation
query.explanation: `&&` returns the first operand when that operand is falsy, and it does not evaluate the second. The returned value is the number 0, not the boolean false and not "value". `||` on the same operands would return "value".

query.title: Logical OR operator and operand selection
query.explanation: The empty string is falsy, so `||` skips it and returns "fallback". It does not return a boolean, and it does not keep the empty string. `??` would keep "", because an empty string is not null or undefined.

questions.prompt: What happens if you assign a new value to a `const` binding?

choices.text: n stays 1 and the assignment is ignored

query.title: const declarations and binding rules
query.explanation: A `const` binding cannot be assigned again after its initializer runs. The second assignment throws a TypeError at runtime. It is not a SyntaxError, because the statement is grammatically valid, and it is not a silent no-op.

questions.prompt: What happens when you change a property of an object held by `const`?

query.title: const does not freeze the object
query.syntax:
const obj = { a: 1 };
obj.a = 2;  // obj.a is 2
query.explanation: `const` protects the binding, not the value. Replacing `obj` with another object would throw, but writing `obj.a` mutates the existing object and leaves the binding in place. `Object.freeze` is what would reject the property write.

questions.prompt: What happens when you read a `let` before its declaration line?

query.title: Block-scoped declarations and the temporal dead zone
query.explanation: A `let` binding exists for the whole block, but it stays uninitialized until its declaration line runs. Reading it in that temporal dead zone throws a ReferenceError. It does not evaluate to undefined the way a `var` binding does, and the declaration is not a syntax error.

questions.prompt: What does reading a `var` before its declaration line produce?

query.title: Variable declarations and hoisting
query.explanation: A `var` declaration is hoisted to the top of its function and initialized to undefined immediately. The assignment `value = 1` still happens on the original line, so an earlier read sees undefined rather than 1. It does not throw the ReferenceError that `let` throws in the same position.

questions.prompt: How do `var` and `let` differ when both are declared inside an `if` block?

choices.text: Both names are visible only inside the block
var is visible throughout the function; let is visible only inside the block
Both names are visible throughout the function
let is visible throughout the function; var is visible only inside the block

query.title: Variable declaration scope: var, let, and blocks
query.explanation: `var` is scoped to the enclosing function, so `a` remains visible after the `if` block ends. `let` is scoped to the block, so `b` cannot be read outside that block. Swapping those two scopes is the usual mix-up with `var`.

questions.prompt: What does this template literal evaluate to?

query.title: Template literals and expression interpolation
query.explanation: A template literal evaluates each `${...}` expression and inserts its string form into the result. The expression `"Ada"` becomes the text Ada between "Hello, " and the end. A normal single-quoted or double-quoted string would have left `${"Ada"}` as characters, and the template is not a syntax error.

questions.prompt: What does a template nested inside another template evaluate to?

query.title: Template literals and substitutions
query.explanation: The inner template is just an expression in the outer `${...}`, so it runs first and produces "b 2". The outer template then inserts that string, producing "a b 2". Nesting is legal. The outer template does not leave the inner backticks uninterpolated.

questions.prompt: What does `String.raw` do with `\n` in the template?

choices.text: A string of one newline character
The string "n", with the backslash dropped
A two-character string: backslash, then n

query.title: Tagged templates and raw strings
query.explanation: `String.raw` returns the template's raw contents, so the characters backslash and n stay as two characters instead of becoming a newline. A normal template literal would turn `\n` into one newline character. `${...}` interpolation still runs inside `String.raw`; only escape processing is skipped.

questions.prompt: What does `map` do to the array it is called on?
questions.code:
const items = [1, 2];
const doubled = items.map((n) => n * 2);

choices.text: It mutates items and returns that same array
It returns a new array and leaves items unchanged
It mutates items in place and returns undefined
It returns an iterator over the doubled values

query.title: Array.prototype.map: callback transformation over arrays
query.explanation: `map` allocates a new array and fills it with whatever the callback returns. It does not write those return values back into the receiver, so the original length and slots stay as they were. Treating `map` as an in-place loop that assigns `items[i] = ...` is the wrong model. A callback can still mutate an object element, because the new array holds the same object references.

query.title: Array filter with a built-in function as predicate
query.explanation: `filter` keeps an element when the callback's return value is truthy, and it drops the element when that return value is falsy. `Boolean` is falsy for 0 and "", so those two are removed and `[1, 2]` remains. The test is truthiness of the callback result, not a required `=== true`, and the original array is not edited in place.

choices.text: The first match's index, or -1 if none
An array of every match, or [] if none
The first match, or undefined if none
The first match, or null if none

query.title: Array.prototype.find and related search methods
query.explanation: `find` returns the first element for which the callback is truthy. If no element passes, it returns undefined, not -1 and not an empty array. `findIndex` is the method that returns an index or -1, and `filter` is the one that returns a new array of every match.

questions.prompt: What does `findIndex` return when nothing matches?

query.title: Array searching methods: find, findIndex and friends
query.explanation: `findIndex` returns the index of the first element whose callback is truthy. When nothing matches, the result is -1, the same sentinel `indexOf` uses. It does not return undefined; that sentinel belongs to `find`, which returns the element itself.

query.title: Array membership testing with includes
query.explanation: `includes` answers whether a value is present and always returns a boolean. It does not return the index or the element. It uses SameValueZero, so `[NaN].includes(NaN)` is true, unlike `indexOf`, which uses strict equality and misses NaN.

questions.prompt: What does `indexOf` return when the value is absent?

query.title: Array.prototype.indexOf search semantics
query.explanation: `indexOf` returns the first matching index, or -1 when nothing matches. The miss result is not undefined, false, or null. The search uses strict equality, so `[NaN].indexOf(NaN)` is also -1 even though a NaN element is present. `includes` is the boolean check, and it does find NaN.

query.title: Array mutator methods and their return values
query.explanation: `push` appends the arguments and returns the array's length after the append. It does mutate `items`, but the return value is the number 2, not the array and not the pushed element. Chaining `.push().push()` fails because that number has no `push` method.

query.title: Array mutator methods and their return values
query.explanation: `pop` removes the last element and returns that element, so `[1, 2].pop()` returns 2 and leaves `[1]`. It does not return the shortened array. On an empty array, `pop` returns undefined rather than throwing.

query.title: Array mutator methods and their return values
query.explanation: `shift` removes the element at index 0, shifts the rest down, and returns the removed element. `[1, 2].shift()` therefore returns 1, not 2 and not the remaining array. An empty array yields undefined, the same miss value as `pop`.

query.title: Array mutator methods at the front of an array
query.explanation: `unshift` inserts arguments at the front and returns the length afterward. The return value is 2, not the array and not the inserted 0, even though `items` does become `[0, 1]`. That return contract matches `push`, not `shift`.

query.title: Array.prototype.slice basics
query.explanation: `slice` copies a range into a new array and leaves the receiver alone, so `items` is still `[1, 2, 3]` while `part` is `[2, 3]`. The end index is exclusive, and a negative index counts from the end. `splice` is the method that edits the original array.

questions.prompt: What do `removed` and `items` hold after this `splice`?

choices.text: removed is [2] and items is still [1, 2, 3]
removed is 2 and items is still [1, 2, 3]

query.title: Array.prototype.splice
query.explanation: `splice` edits the original array and returns an array of the deleted elements. Deleting one element still returns a one-element array, `[2]`, not the bare number 2 that `pop` would return. `items` becomes `[1, 3]`. A delete count of 0 returns an empty array and can still insert.

choices.text: next is [1, 2] and items is still [1]
next and items are the same array

query.title: Array.prototype.concat and array identity
query.explanation: `concat` builds a new array and does not append into the receiver, so `items` stays `[1]` and `next` is `[1, 2]`. The two names do not point at one array. Array arguments are flattened one level only: `[1].concat([2, [3]])` is `[1, 2, [3]]`, not a fully flat list.

questions.prompt: After this spread copy, what is `inner.n`?

query.title: Spread syntax for copying arrays
query.explanation: Spreading an array allocates a new array and copies the element references into it. The object `inner` is not cloned, so `copy[0]` and `inner` are the same object and the write to `n` is visible through both. A change to `copy.length` or a replacement of `copy[0]` would not rewrite the source array. Spread is not a deep copy.

query.title: Object spread syntax in object literals
query.explanation: Object spread copies enumerable own string properties from left to right. When `b` appears again, the later value 3 overwrites the earlier 2, and `a` stays 1. A "first key wins" reading is backwards. Non-enumerable properties and symbol keys are not copied by spread at all.

questions.prompt: What are `a` and `b` after these destructuring defaults?

choices.text: a is null and b is null
a is 1 and b is null
a is undefined and b is null

query.title: Default values in array destructuring
query.explanation: A destructuring default runs when the element is undefined, including when the element is missing. `undefined` is replaced by 1, but `null` is a present value, so `b` stays null. 0 and "" would also be kept. The default is not a stand-in for every falsy element.

questions.prompt: What are `a` and `b` in this pattern?

query.title: Array destructuring with skipped elements
query.explanation: An elision in an array pattern, the extra comma, skips that source element. `a` receives 1, the 2 is discarded, and `b` receives 3. The hole is not a syntax error, and it does not create a binding whose value is 2.

query.title: Array destructuring with a rest element
query.explanation: A rest element in array destructuring gathers every remaining value into a new array. `head` is 1 and `tail` is `[2, 3]`, not the single number 2. If nothing remains, the rest binding is an empty array, not undefined. The rest element has to be last in the pattern.

questions.prompt: Which binding does `const { a: b } = { a: 1 }` create?

query.title: Object destructuring with renaming
query.explanation: In `{ a: b }`, `a` is the property to read and `b` is the local binding that receives it. The pattern declares `b`, set to 1, and does not declare `a`. Reading it as "a is 1" swaps the source property with the new name. The colon here is not a default and not a type annotation.

questions.prompt: What are `a` and `b` after these object defaults?
questions.code:
const { a = 1 } = { a: null };
const { b = 1 } = {};

choices.text: a is null and b is 1
a is null and b is undefined
a is 1 and b is undefined

query.title: Default values in object destructuring
query.explanation: An object-destructuring default replaces a property only when that property's value is undefined. An explicit `null` is kept, so `a` is null. A missing property counts as undefined, so `b` becomes 1. Falsy values such as 0 and "" are kept as well.

query.title: Object destructuring assignment and defaults
query.explanation: Object destructuring reads the named property and, when it is absent, binds undefined. It does not throw just because the key is missing. A default is what would replace that undefined. Destructuring `null` or `undefined` as the whole source is the case that throws.

query.title: Object destructuring and what it can be applied to
query.explanation: Destructuring requires the source to be coercible to an object. `null` and `undefined` fail that check and throw a TypeError before any property is read. A missing property on a real object does not throw; it binds undefined. Optional chaining is a different operator and is not implied by a destructuring pattern.

questions.prompt: In an object literal, `{ name }` means `{ name: name }`.

query.title: Object literal shorthand syntax
query.explanation: Shorthand property syntax uses the identifier both as the key and as the value expression. `{ name }` is the same object as `{ name: name }`, so `person.name` is "Ada". It does not create a key with the value undefined, and it is not a destructuring pattern: that same brace shape on the left of `=` would unpack instead of build.

questions.prompt: A computed property name evaluates its expression.

query.title: Object literal property names from bracketed expressions
query.explanation: Brackets around a property name evaluate the expression and use the result as the key. `key` holds "id", so the object is `{ id: 1 }`, not an object whose key is the identifier "key". The expression can be any value that converts to a property key, including string concatenation such as `["a" + "b"]`.

query.title: Iterating with for...of loops
query.explanation: `for...of` pulls values from the iterable protocol. On an array, the loop variable is "a" and then "b", the elements, not the index strings "0" and "1". `for...in` is the loop that yields keys. A plain object is not iterable, so `for...of` on `{}` throws.

questions.prompt: `for...in` yields enumerable string keys, including inherited ones.

query.title: for...in loop and property enumeration
query.explanation: `for...in` enumerates enumerable string keys on the object and continues up the prototype chain, so both "own" and "inherited" appear. It does not yield values, and it skips non-enumerable properties and symbol keys. `Object.keys` is the own-only list, so an inherited enumerable key shows up in `for...in` and not in `Object.keys`.

questions.prompt: `for...in` on an array yields the indexes as strings.

query.title: Enumerating keys with for...in
query.explanation: Array indexes are property keys, and property keys that `for...in` visits are strings. The loop variable is "0" and then "1", not the numbers 0 and 1, and not the elements "a" and "b". `for...of` is what yields the elements. Other enumerable keys, including inherited ones, are visited too.

questions.prompt: `JSON.stringify` omits object keys whose value is `undefined`.

query.title: JSON.stringify value serialization rules
query.explanation: JSON has no undefined value. When an object property is undefined, `JSON.stringify` leaves that key out, so the result is '{"a":1}'. The key is not serialized as null. An undefined element inside an array is handled differently: that slot becomes null rather than disappearing.

questions.prompt: `JSON.stringify` turns an array hole, or an `undefined` element, into `null`.

query.title: JSON.stringify serialization of unsupported values
query.explanation: In an array, both an explicit undefined element and a hole are serialized as null, so the slot stays in the JSON text. That differs from object properties, where undefined keys are omitted entirely. The array does not shrink, and the element is not left as the token undefined, which is not valid JSON.

questions.prompt: `JSON.stringify` omits function-valued properties of an object.

query.title: JSON.stringify value serialization rules
query.explanation: Functions are not JSON values. `JSON.stringify` drops a function-valued property of an object the same way it drops undefined, so `b` is absent and the result is '{"a":1}'. A function element of an array is not dropped: that slot becomes null. The function source is never written into the JSON.

questions.prompt: `JSON.parse` of a JSON string returns the value that string describes.

query.title: Parsing JSON text into JavaScript values
query.explanation: `JSON.parse` reads JSON text and returns the corresponding value: an object, array, string, number, boolean, or null. `JSON.parse('{"a":1}').a` is the number 1, not a leftover string. Invalid JSON throws a SyntaxError. The reviver argument can rewrite values, but the default call returns the parsed data.

questions.prompt: An arrow function cannot be constructed with `new`.

query.title: The new operator and constructible functions
query.explanation: Arrow functions do not have a `[[Construct]]` internal method and do not get a `prototype` property. Calling one with `new` throws a TypeError. A `function` declaration or expression can be constructed with `new`. The arrow still runs fine as an ordinary call.

questions.prompt: An arrow function does not bind its own `arguments` object.

query.title: Function scope objects and lexical binding in functions
query.explanation: An arrow function does not create an `arguments` binding for its own parameters. At the top of a module, `arguments` is unresolved, so calling that arrow throws a ReferenceError. Nested inside a traditional function, the arrow sees that outer `arguments` object lexically, which lists the outer function's arguments, not the arrow's.

questions.prompt: A function declaration is hoisted within its scope.

query.title: Declaration hoisting and creation order
query.explanation: A function declaration is initialized for the whole of its scope before that scope starts running, so a call on an earlier line succeeds. In strict mode the scope is the enclosing block or function, and the name does not leak out of that block. A `const` function expression does not get this treatment: touching it early throws.

questions.prompt: A function expression assigned to `const` is in the temporal dead zone before its line.

query.title: let/const hoisting and initialization timing
query.explanation: The `const` binding is hoisted but uninitialized, so a call before the declaration line throws a ReferenceError. The function value does not exist until that line runs. This is not the TypeError you would get from `var expression = function () {}`, where the hoisted binding is undefined and you try to call it. A function declaration, by contrast, can be called earlier in the same scope.

questions.prompt: A default parameter is used for `undefined`, and not for `null`.

query.title: Default function parameters
query.explanation: A default parameter initializer runs when the argument is undefined, including when the caller omits it. `f(undefined)` therefore returns 1. `null` is a passed value, so `f(null)` returns null and the default does not run. The same rule rejects the idea that every falsy argument, such as 0, is replaced.

questions.prompt: A default parameter may read an earlier parameter.

query.title: Default parameter initializers and scope
query.explanation: Default expressions are evaluated left to right in a scope where earlier parameters are already initialized. `f(4)` leaves `b` undefined, so the default reads `a` and returns 4. A default cannot read a later parameter: that binding is still in the temporal dead zone, and the initializer throws a ReferenceError if it runs.

questions.prompt: `switch` compares the discriminant with each `case` using `===`.

query.title: switch statement case matching
query.explanation: Each `case` label is compared with the discriminant using `===`. The number 1 does not match the string "1", so that branch is skipped. There is no `ToNumber` coercion the way `==` would apply. The comparison is not a truthiness test of the case label.

questions.prompt: `switch` falls through to the next case when `break` is omitted.

query.title: switch statement case matching and control flow
query.explanation: Once a `case` matches, execution continues into the following cases until a `break`, a `return`, or the end of the switch. Matching `case 1` and omitting `break` also runs the body of `case 2`. Cases are not isolated blocks. A `break` is what stops that fall-through.

query.title: The void operator
query.explanation: The `void` operator evaluates its operand, discards that value, and returns undefined. `void 0` is undefined, and a side effect inside the operand still happens. It does not delete a binding, and it does not return 0. The operand expression runs; only its result is thrown away.

questions.prompt: `delete` returns `true` when it removes a configurable own property.

query.title: The delete operator and property descriptors
query.explanation: A property created by an ordinary assignment is configurable. `delete obj.a` removes that own property and returns true. In strict mode, deleting a non-configurable property throws a TypeError instead of returning false. `delete` also returns true when the property was already absent, so true alone does not prove a field was there.

questions.prompt: `delete` on an array index leaves a hole and does not change `length`.

query.title: The delete operator on object properties and array elements
query.explanation: `delete items[1]` removes the own property at that index and returns true, but `length` stays 3. The index is then a hole: `1 in items` is false, while a direct read of `items[1]` is undefined. `splice(1, 1)` is what would close the gap and set `length` to 2. `delete` does not reindex the tail.

questions.prompt: The `in` operator is `true` for an inherited property.

query.title: The `in` operator and property lookup
query.explanation: The `in` operator returns true when the property is found on the object or anywhere on its prototype chain. `toString` lives on `Object.prototype`, so `"toString" in {}` is true even though `{}` has no own properties. `Object.hasOwn({}, "toString")` is false. `in` is not a check of the property's value.

query.title: Own-property checks with Object.hasOwn
query.explanation: `Object.hasOwn` returns true only for an own property, whether or not that property is enumerable. `"toString" in {}` is true because of the prototype, but `Object.hasOwn({}, "toString")` is false. It does not invoke an instance method named `hasOwnProperty`, so a shadowed `hasOwnProperty` on the object cannot change the result.

query.title: Property enumeration and own-key listing methods
query.explanation: `Object.keys` returns an array of the object's own enumerable string keys. A non-enumerable property such as "hidden" is left out, and a symbol key is left out, so the list is `["visible"]`. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` includes non-enumerable string keys, and `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` lists symbol keys. Inherited enumerable names are omitted too.

query.title: Math.max and Math.min argument handling
query.explanation: With no arguments, `Math.max` returns `-Infinity`, the identity value for maximum, so adding it to a later comparison cannot raise the result. It does not throw, and it does not return 0 or undefined. `Math.min()` with no arguments is the opposite identity, `Infinity`.

query.title: Spread syntax in function calls vs passing an array argument
query.explanation: `Math.max` converts each argument with `ToNumber`. One array argument becomes `ToNumber([1, 2, 3])`, the array stringifies to "1,2,3", and that is NaN. Spreading passes three separate numbers, and the greatest is 3. An empty array is a different input: `Math.max([])` is 0, because an empty array converts to 0.

query.title: The + operator with mixed operand types
query.explanation: If either operand of `+` is a string, both sides are converted to strings and concatenated. The number 1 becomes "1", so the result is the string "51", not the number 6. Subtraction does not have a string mode: `'5' - 1` is the number 4. Evaluation is left to right, so `1 + 1 + "5"` is "25".

query.title: Implicit type coercion with arithmetic operators
query.explanation: The `-` operator converts both operands with `ToNumber` and subtracts. `ToNumber("5")` is 5, so the result is the number 4, not the string "4" and not NaN. `+` is the operator that would have concatenated these operands into "51". A string that is not numeric, such as "5px", becomes NaN under subtraction.

query.title: The + operator and implicit type conversion
query.explanation: Neither operand of `+` is a string, so both are converted with `ToNumber`. `ToNumber(true)` is 1, and `1 + 1` is the number 2, not the boolean true. `true + false` is 1 by the same rule. `Boolean` context is unrelated: this expression never asks whether the sum is truthy.

questions.prompt: Which function returns a copy of an array of numbers sorted from smallest to largest?

choices.rationale: With no comparator, sort() converts the numbers to strings and compares them as text, so 10 sorts before 9.

criterion.statement: Sorts every array of numbers into ascending numeric order.

query.title: Array.prototype.sort and comparator functions
query.explanation: Without a comparator, `sort()` converts every element to a string and orders them by UTF-16 code units, so `[10, 9, 1]` becomes `[1, 10, 9]`. Pass `(a, b) => a - b` to sort numbers by value.

questions.prompt: Which function returns true only when its argument is the number 0?

choices.rationale: == converts its operands first, so the empty string, '0', and [] all compare equal to 0.

criterion.statement: Returns true for the number 0 and false for every other value.
criterion.evidence: Fails for input "": expected false, got true

query.title: Equality operators: == versus ===
query.explanation: Loose equality converts both sides to a common type before comparing, so `'' == 0`, `'0' == 0`, and `[] == 0` are all true. Strict equality compares type and value with no conversion, which is what a check for one specific value needs.

questions.prompt: Both snippets count how many of 2,000 numbers are in an allowed collection of 10,000. Which is faster?

choices.rationale: includes() scans the array from the start on every call, so each lookup here walks through about 9,000 items.

criterion.statement: Faster median run time on the same input.
criterion.evidence: A: 0.6 ms, B: 3.1 ms median on Node 24.21.0

query.title: Membership lookup in Set vs Array
query.explanation: `array.includes(x)` is a linear scan. A `Set` is a hash table, so `set.has(x)` takes about the same time however many items it holds. For repeated lookups, build the Set once.

questions.prompt: Both snippets double 2,000 numbers into a new array. Which is faster?

choices.text: reduce() that spreads the accumulator each step
choices.code:
const values = Array.from({ length: 2000 }, (_, i) => i);
const doubled = values.reduce((result, value) => [...result, value * 2], []);
choices.rationale: Spreading the accumulator copies every element built so far on each step, so the reduce is quadratic.

choices.code:
const values = Array.from({ length: 2000 }, (_, i) => i);
const doubled = values.map((value) => value * 2);

criterion.statement: Faster median run time on the same input.
criterion.evidence: A: 2.6 ms, B: 0.094 ms median on Node 24.21.0

query.title: Building arrays: reduce, map, and copying costs
query.explanation: `[...result, value]` allocates a new array and copies all of `result` into it. Doing that once per element copies about n * n / 2 elements in total. `map()` writes each result once.
